meta.title: Split a box until the pieces are small enough
meta.description: RECURSIVE SUBDIVISION WITHOUT RECURSION, which is the third thing this corpus does with `repeatUntil` and the one that looks least like a loop. A split grammar is normally written as a function that calls itself on each half; a subgraph here may not reference itself, so the same structure is spelled as a loop whose carry is THE WHOLE SET OF CELLS and whose body replaces every open cell with its two halves. What comes back is the leaves -- the cells nothing wanted to split again -- and the tree that produced them is gone, which is exactly what a facade needs. A CELL IS A POINT, and the box it stands for is the `boundsMin`/`boundsMax` pair every point in this library already carries. Nothing new had to be represented: the standard bounds columns ARE the cell, `setBounds` is field-capable per point so the two halves are computed in one node, and the split rule is ordinary arithmetic over them. THE FAN-OUT IS `repeatPoints` WITH `count` 2: every open cell is emitted twice, the copies are numbered 0 and 1 in `slot`, and every column the cell has -- its box, its depth, the decisions already made on it -- rides onto both copies with no carry list to keep. The copies are coincident, so a child lands exactly on its parent and `slot` alone decides which half it becomes. THE SPLIT READS THE BOX THE CELL ARRIVED WITH, in the same node that rewrites it: `setBounds` resolves both corners against its input before writing either, so the field for one corner never sees the other corner this cook just wrote, and the parent's box needs no second copy under other names. THE AXIS IS ARGMAX OF THE THREE SPANS, and the grammar has no `argmax` and no `and` -- `mul` is AND on 0/1 predicates, so the x flag is `ge(sx,sy) * ge(sx,sz)` and the later flags subtract the ones already claimed, which makes the three mutually exclusive without a branch. They are written as one 0/1 vec3, `axis`. Splitting the LONGEST span is what keeps the cells from degenerating into slivers: split a fixed axis and every cell ends up as tall as the facade and a finger wide. It is also why this reads as a flat panel with no third dimension named anywhere -- the root box is 0.4 deep, so Z is never the longest span and never gets chosen. WHERE TO CUT IS THE PARENT'S DECISION, and it is the easiest thing here to get wrong. The two halves of one cell have DIFFERENT seeds -- `repeatPoints` gives copy k of a point the seed hashCombine(seed, k), which is what keeps coincident copies two points rather than one -- so a fraction drawn on each CHILD, after the fan-out, would come out different in the two halves and cut them at two different coordinates: one half would end at one, the other would begin at the other, and the strip between them would belong to neither half or to both. Nothing would fail: every cell would still be a valid box and the picture would still look like a subdivided panel. Measured on this graph at its own seed, with `where` moved after `repeatPoints`: 82.9 of the 360 square units would be covered by no leaf and 198.4 more would be covered more than once (128.4 square units lie under two or more leaves), the leaves summing to 475.5. That is not hypothetical history: the graph was first written, on `copyToPoints`, with the fraction drawn on the child. The rule is that a decision SHARED by the children is made on the parent and carried down, and only a decision that differs per child may be drawn after the fan-out. The axis and the cut are both shared, so `axis` and `where` write them on the open cell BEFORE `repeatPoints` -- `where` stores the cut as a coordinate, `cutAt`, the parent's low corner along the chosen axis plus a fraction in [0.34, 0.66) of its span -- and the split only reads them back: each component of each corner is `select(axis_i * slot, cutAt, boundsMin_i)` for the low corner and `select(axis_i * (1 - slot), cutAt, boundsMax_i)` for the high one, so the upper half's low corner and the lower half's high corner move to the cut on the chosen axis and everything else keeps the parent's value. Both halves read the one stored `cutAt`, so they meet at the same f32 coordinate and the leaves tile the root exactly -- no gap, no overlap, a summed area of 360 against a root of 360 -- which is the assertion worth making about a subdivision and the one a picture cannot make for you. Deciding on the parent is also what keeps the split small: the argmax and the cut are spelled once, where computing them inside `setBounds` would repeat the whole expression under every component of both corners. IT STOPS ON A SIZE FLOOR AND A DEPTH CAP: a cell stays open while its longest span exceeds 1.7 and its depth is under 9. The floor alone would end the loop -- each half keeps between 34% and 66% of the span it was cut from, so the longest span shrinks geometrically and no sliver can outrun it; with the cap removed and the round limit raised, every seed from 0 to 199 settles by depth 11 with at most 299 cells. The cap is a choice about the picture, not a guard against running forever: it binds in 198 of those 200 seeds, stopping about nine cells per facade (at most 18) while their longest span is still above 1.7, so the finest corners of the panel stop a split or two early. A depth cap alone would not do instead: it leaves the cells of a wide facade still wide. Settling sums the 0/1 `live` flag into the detail domain -- mode `count` reports the element count and ignores the attribute named, so over a set of cells that only grows it never reaches zero. WHAT IT IS NOT: a grammar. Every cell splits by the same rule, so this makes a Mondrian rather than a facade with a stated vocabulary of bays and openings. Giving a cell a KIND, and choosing the rule by that kind, is the next thing and wants `byAttribute` over a string; nothing here is in its way.
